title: The Tell-Tale Heart
focus: guilt that the mind cannot hide

teacherSummary.text: An unnamed narrator insists he is sane while describing how the old man's pale blue 'vulture eye' drove him to murder. He spies on the old man for seven nights, kills him on the eighth, dismembers the body and hides it under the floorboards. When police arrive he chats calmly, but a beating sound he believes is the dead man's heart grows louder until he shrieks a confession.

context.history: Poe published the story in 1843. Insanity was a live legal question: the 1843 M'Naghten case in Britain set the test for an insanity defense in the same year. Poe's narrators often argue their own case.

significance: It is one of the most taught examples of an unreliable first-person narrator; every claim of calm reason undercuts itself.
discussionQuestions: The narrator keeps telling us he is not mad. Why might someone insist so hard on a point?
Where does point of view appear in this story, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this story connect to the book's larger concern with guilt and conscience?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Tell-Tale Heart,” how does Poe show guilt that the mind cannot hide? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Tell-Tale Heart, how does Poe develop the idea of guilt that the mind cannot hide? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Tell-Tale Heart develops the idea of guilt that the mind cannot hide. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Tell-Tale Heart (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of guilt that the mind cannot hide. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Tell-Tale Heart suggests about guilt that the mind cannot hide. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's point of view and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Edgar Allan Poe uses point of view in The Tell-Tale Heart to complicate the reader's understanding of guilt that the mind cannot hide. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Tell-Tale Heart within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of guilt that the mind cannot hide responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Tell-Tale Heart alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of guilt that the mind cannot hide follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Tell-Tale Heart and its treatment of guilt that the mind cannot hide. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's point of view and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Tell-Tale Heart as evidence for a larger claim about guilt that the mind cannot hide in The Tell-Tale Heart. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Tell-Tale Heart as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of guilt that the mind cannot hide. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Tell-Tale Heart.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: The narrator keeps telling us he is not mad. Why might someone insist so hard on a point? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Heads-up: this story includes murder and dismemberment, described briefly.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are dismembered, suavity, dissemble, dissimulation, uncontrollable. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “First of all I dismembered the corpse.” In this sentence it means: cut a body into pieces. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of The Tell-Tale Heart would have known. Poe published the story in 1843. Insanity was a live legal question: the 1843 M'Naghten case in Britain set the test for an insanity defense in the same year. Poe's narrators often argue their own case. Why does this story matter? It is one of the most taught examples of an unreliable first-person narrator; every claim of calm reason undercuts itself. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “I kept quite still and said nothing.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to guilt that the mind cannot hide? I circle “watches”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find point of view, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for point of view.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: I kept quite still and said nothing. For a whole hour I did not move a muscle, and in the mean time I did not hear him lie down. He was still sitting up in the bed, listening;—just as I have done, night after night, hearkening to the death watches in the wall.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Irony, Imagery: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how The Tell-Tale Heart develops the idea of guilt that the mind cannot hide. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to guilt and conscience? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about guilt that the mind cannot hide, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes guilt that the mind cannot hide. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
